item.text: {"text":"Recent work supports history interventions as diagnostics of sequential recommenders. [Scarcelli et al. (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.03606) search for minimal interaction-history edits that change recommendations using a genetic algorithm, directly motivating recommendation-flip and target-rank probes. [CoDeR (AAAI 2025)](https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/AAAI/article/view/33379) addresses demand shifts obscured by noise and bias through demand extraction and counterfactual reasoning. These approaches motivate sensitivity analysis, but do not establish that deleting recent or repeated interactions identifies users’ causal preferences.\n\nSuggested diagnostic design: compare intact histories with removal of recent interactions, older interactions, and interactions representing repeated interests. Pair each intervention with equal-count random removals across several seeds; hold candidate sets and model weights fixed. Measure final-position target-rank changes, score-margin changes, top-10 overlap, and recommendation flips. Separate deletion with sequence compaction from position-preserving masking, since shifting positions can itself change predictions. Define repeated interests using observed item recurrence or transparent title/description similarity; report unavailable or empty groups explicitly. Excess sensitivity beyond random-removal controls indicates dependence on particular history content. Improved target rankings after removing adjacent-interest interactions would support an interference hypothesis; distinguishing sequence-encoding effects from training-signal effects still requires controlled architecture or loss ablations. These are proposed probes, not established findings from the cited papers."}
